entries.6db73f6fff4c0b09ec05d74bdbfe737ea0d18223: <div sID="gen33255" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Jas.2" sID="Jas.2"/> <div eID="gen33255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33256" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33257" type="x-p"/> In this chapter the apostle condemns a sinful regarding of the rich, and despising the poor, which he imputes to partiality and injustice, and shows it to be an acting contrary to God, who has chosen the poor, and whose interest is often persecuted, and his name blasphemed, by the rich, <reference osisRef="Jas.2.1-Jas.2.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. He shows that the whole law is to be fulfilled, and that mercy should be followed, as well as justice, <reference osisRef="Jas.2.8-Jas.2.13">ver. 8-13</reference>. He exposes the error and folly of those who boast of faith without works, telling us that this is but a dead faith, and such a faith as devils have, not the faith of Abraham, or of Rahab, <reference osisRef="Jas.2.11-Jas.2.26">ver. 11, to the end</reference>.
entries.77d8e0e40b54389096aec2c3d8d32a8b7ff7540b: <div eID="gen33257" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33256" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Regard Due to Poor Christians; Partiality Condemned. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 61.)</title> <div sID="gen33258" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, <hi type="italic">the Lord</hi> of glory, with respect of persons. 2 For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment; <hi type="super">3</hi> And ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing, and say unto him, Sit thou here in a good place; and say to the poor, Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool: 4 Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts? <hi type="super">5</hi> Hearken, my beloved brethren, Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he hath promised to them that love him? <hi type="super">6</hi> But ye have despised the poor. Do not rich men oppress you, and draw you before the judgment seats? <hi type="super">7</hi> Do not they blaspheme that worthy name by the which ye are called? <div eID="gen33258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33259" type="x-p"/> The apostle is here reproving a very corrupt practice. He shows how much mischief there is in the sin of <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">prosopolepsia</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">respect of persons,</hi> which seemed to be a very growing evil in the churches of Christ even in those early ages, and which, in these after-times, has sadly corrupted and divided Christian nations and societies. Here we have, <div eID="gen33259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33260" type="x-p"/> I. A caution against this sin laid down in general: <hi type="italic">My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.1">v. 1</reference>. Observe here, 1. The character of Christians fully implied: they are such as have the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ; they embrace it; they receive it; they govern themselves by it; they entertain the doctrine, and submit to the law and government, of Christ; they have it as a trust; they have it as a treasure. 2. How honorably James speaks of Jesus Christ; he calls him <hi type="italic">the Lord of glory;</hi> for he is <hi type="italic">the brightness of his Father's glory, and the express image of his person.</hi> 3. Christ's being the Lord of glory should teach us not to respect Christians for any thing so much as their relation and conformity to Christ. You who profess to believe the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, which the poorest Christian shall partake of equally with the rich, and to which all worldly glory is but vanity, you should not make men's outward and worldly advantages the measure of your respect. In professing the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, we should not show respect to men, so as to cloud or lessen the glory of our glorious Lord: how ever any may think of it, this is certainly a very heinous sin. <div eID="gen33260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33261" type="x-p"/> II. We have this sin described and cautioned against, by an instance or example of it (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.2-Jas.2.3">v. 2, 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">For if there come into your assembly a man with a gold ring,</hi> &c. <hi type="italic">Assembly</hi> here is meant of those meetings which were appointed for deciding matters of difference among the members of the church, or for determining when censures should be passed upon any, and what those censures should be; therefore the Greek word here used, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">synagoge,</hi></hi> signifies such an assembly as that in the Jewish synagogues, when they met to do justice. Maimonides says (as I find the passage quoted by Dr. Manton) "That is was expressly provided by the Jews' constitutions that, when a poor man and a rich plead together, the rich shall not be bidden to sit down and the poor stand, or sit in a worse place, but both sit or both stand alike." To this the phrases used by the apostle have a most plain reference, and therefore the assembly here spoken of must be some such as the synagogue-assemblies of the Jews were, when they met to hear causes and to execute justice: to these the arbitrations and censures of their Christian assemblies are compared. But we must be careful not to apply what is here said to the common assemblies for worship; for in these certainly there may be appointed different places of persons according to their rank and circumstances, without sin. Those do not understand the apostle who fix his severity here upon this practice; they do not consider the word judges (used in <reference osisRef="Jas.2.4">v. 4</reference>), nor what is said of their being convected as transgressors of the law, if they had such a respect of persons as is here spoken of, according to <reference osisRef="Jas.2.9">v. 9</reference>. Thus, now put the case: "<hi type="italic">There comes into your assembly</hi> (when of the same nature with some of those at the synagogue) <hi type="italic">a man</hi> that is distinguished by his dress, and who makes a figure, <hi type="italic">and there comes in also a poor man in vile raiment,</hi> and you act partially, and determine wrong, merely because the one makes a better appearance, or is in better circumstances, than the other." Observe hence, 1. God has his remnant among all sorts of people, among those that wear soft and gay clothing, and among those that wear poor and vile raiment. 2. In matters of religion, rich and poor stand upon a level; no man's riches set him in the least nearer to God, nor does any man's poverty set him at a distance from God. <hi type="italic">With the Most High there is no respect of persons,</hi> and therefore in matters of conscience there should be none with us. 3. All undue honouring of worldly greatness and riches should especially be watched against in Christian societies. James does not here encourage rudeness or disorder. Civil respect must be paid, and some difference may be allowed in our carriage towards persons of different ranks; but this respect must never be such as to influence the proceedings of Christian societies in disposing of the offices of the church, or in passing the censures of the church, or in any thing that is purely a matter of religion; here we are to know no man after the flesh. It is the character of a citizen of Zion that <hi type="italic">in his eyes a vile person is contemned, but he honoureth those that fear the Lord.</hi> If a poor man be a good man, we must not value him a whit the less for his poverty; and, if a rich man be a bad man (though he may have both gay clothing and a gay profession), we must not value him any whit the more for his riches. 4. Of what importance it is to take care what rule we go by in judging of men; if we allow ourselves commonly to judge by outward appearance, this will too much influence our spirits and our conduct in religious assemblies. There is many a man, whose wickedness renders him vile and despicable, who yet makes a figure in the world; and, on the other hand, there is many a humble, heavenly, good Christian, who is clothed meanly; but neither should he nor his Christianity be thought the worse of on this account. <div eID="gen33261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33262" type="x-p"/> III. We have the greatness of this sin set forth, <reference osisRef="Jas.2.4-Jas.2.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. It is great partiality, it is injustice, and it is to set ourselves against God, who has chosen the poor, and will honour and advance them (if good), let who will despise them. 1. In this sin there is shameful partiality: <hi type="italic">Are you not then partial in yourselves?</hi> The question is here put, as what could not fail of being answered by every man's conscience that would put it seriously to himself. According to the strict rendering of the original, the question is, "<hi type="italic">Have you not made a difference?</hi> And, in that difference, do you not judge by a false rule, and go upon false measures? And does not the charge of a partiality condemned by the law lie fully against you? Does not your own conscience tell you that you are guilty?" Appeals to conscience are of great advantage, when we have to do with such as make a profession, even though they may have fallen into a very corrupt state. 2. This respect of persons is owing to the evil and injustice of the thoughts. As the temper, conduct, and proceedings, are partial, so the heart and thoughts, from which all flows, are evil: "<hi type="italic">You have become judges of evil thoughts;</hi> that is, you are judges according to those unjust estimations and corrupt opinions which you have formed to yourselves. Trace your partiality till you come to those hidden thoughts which accompany and support it, and you will find those to be <hi type="italic">exceedingly evil.</hi> You secretly prefer outward pomp before inward grace, and the things that are seen before those which are not seen." The deformity of sin is never truly and fully discerned till the evil of our thoughts be disclosed: and it is this which highly aggravates the faults of our tempers and lives—that <hi type="italic">the imagination of the thoughts of the heart is evil,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.6.5">Gen. vi. 5</reference>. 3. This respect of persons is a heinous sin, because it is to show ourselves most directly contrary to God (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Hath not God chosen the poor of this world, rich in faith? &c. But you have despised them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.6">v. 6</reference>. God has made those heirs of a kingdom whom you make of no reputation, and has given very great and glorious promises to those to whom you can hardly give a good word or a respectful look. And is not this a monstrous iniquity in you who pretend to be the children of God and conformed to him? <hi type="italic">Hearken, my beloved brethren;</hi> by all the love I have for you, and all the regards you have to me, I beg you would consider these things. Take notice that many of the poor of this world are the chosen of God. Their being God's chosen does not prevent their being poor; their being poor does not at all prejudice the evidences of their being chosen. <reference osisRef="Matt.11.5">Matt. xi. 5</reference>, <hi type="italic">The poor are evangelized.</hi>" God designed to recommend his holy religion to men's esteem and affection, not by the external advantages of gaiety and pomp, but by its intrinsic worth and excellency; and therefore chose the poor of this world. Again, take notice that many poor of the world are rich in faith; thus the poorest may become rich; and this is what they ought to be especially ambitious of. It is expected from those who have wealth and estates that they be rich in good works, because the more they have the more they have to do good with; but it is expected from the poor in the world that they be rich in faith, for the less they have here the more they may, and should, live in the believing expectation of better things in a better world. Take notice further, Believing Christians are rich in title, and in being heirs of a kingdom, though they may be very poor as to present possessions. What is laid out upon them is but little; what is laid up for them is unspeakably rich and great. Note again, Where any are rich in faith, there will be also divine love; faith working by love will be in all the heirs of glory. Note once more, under this head, Heaven is a kingdom, and a kingdom promised to those that love God. We read of the crown promised to those that love God, in the former chapter (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.12">v. 12</reference>); we here find there is a kingdom too. And, as the crown is a crown of life, so the kingdom will be an everlasting kingdom. All these things, laid together, show how highly the poor in this world, if rich in faith, are now honoured, and shall hereafter be advanced by God; and consequently how very sinful a thing it was for them to despise the poor. After such considerations as these, the charge is cutting indeed: <hi type="italic">But you have despised the poor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.6">v. 6</reference>. 4. Respecting persons, in the sense of this place, on account of their riches or outward figure, is shown to be a very great sin, because of the mischiefs which are owing to worldly wealth and greatness, and the folly which there is in Christians' paying undue regards to those who had so little regard either to their God or them: "<hi type="italic">Do not rich men oppress you, and draw you before the judgment-seat? Do not they blaspheme that worthy name by which you are called?</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.7">v. 7</reference>. Consider how commonly riches are the incentives of vice and mischief, of blasphemy and persecution: consider how many calamities you yourselves sustain, and how great reproaches are thrown upon your religion and your God by men of wealth, and power, and worldly greatness; and this will make your sin appear exceedingly sinful and foolish, in setting up that which tends to pull you down, and to destroy all that you are building up, and to dishonour that worthy name by which you are called." The name of Christ is a worthy name; it reflects honour, and gives worth to those who wear it.
entries.addde567ac7720fe8d9f197c539858576e0a1b67: <div eID="gen33262" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Christian Law. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 61.)</title> <div sID="gen33263" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> If ye fulfil the royal law according to the scripture, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, ye do well: 9 But if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin, and are convinced of the law as transgressors. <hi type="super">10</hi> For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one <hi type="italic">point,</hi> he is guilty of all. <hi type="super">11</hi> For he that said, Do not commit adultery, said also, Do not kill. Now if thou commit no adultery, yet if thou kill, thou art become a transgressor of the law. <hi type="super">12</hi> So speak ye, and so do, as they that shall be judged by the law of liberty. 13 For he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath showed no mercy; and mercy rejoiceth against judgment. <div eID="gen33263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33264" type="x-p"/> The apostle, having condemned the sin of those who had an undue respect of persons, and having urged what was sufficient to convict them of the greatness of this evil, now proceeds to show how the matter may be mended; it is the work of a gospel ministry, not only to reprove and warn, but to teach and direct. <reference osisRef="Col.1.28">Col. i. 28</reference>, <hi type="italic">Warning every man, and teaching every man.</hi> And here, <div eID="gen33264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33265" type="x-p"/> I. We have the law that is to guide us in all our regards to men set down in general. <hi type="italic">If you fulfil the royal law, according to the scripture, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, you do well,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.8">v. 8</reference>. Lest any should think James had been pleading for the poor so as to throw contempt on the rich, he now lets them know that he did not design to encourage improper conduct towards any; they must not hate nor be rude to the rich, any more than despise the poor; but as the scripture teaches us to love all our neighbours, be they rich or poor, as ourselves, so, in our having a steady regard to this rule, <hi type="italic">we shall do well.</hi> Observe hence, 1. The rule for Christians to walk by is settled in the scriptures: <hi type="italic">If according to the scriptures,</hi> &c. It is not great men, nor worldly wealth, nor corrupt practices among professors themselves, that must guide us, but the scriptures of truth. 2. The scripture gives us this as a law, to love our neighbour as ourselves; it is what still remains in full force, and is rather carried higher and further by Christ than made less important to us. 3. This law is a royal law, it comes from the King of kings. Its own worth and dignity deserve it should be thus honoured; and the state in which all Christians now are, as it is a state of liberty, and not of bondage or oppression, makes this law, by which they are to regulate all their actions to one another, a royal law. 4. A pretence of observing this royal law, when it is interpreted with partiality, will not excuse men in any unjust proceedings. In is implied here that some were ready to flatter rich men, and be partial to them, because, if they were in the like circumstances, they should expect such regards to themselves; or they might plead that to show a distinguished respect to those whom God in his providence had distinguished by their rank and degree in the world was but doing right; therefore the apostle allows that, so far as they were concerned to observe the duties of the second table, they <hi type="italic">did well in giving honour to whom honour was due;</hi> but this fair pretence would not cover their sin in that undue <hi type="italic">respect of persons</hi> which they stood chargeable with; for, <div eID="gen33265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33266" type="x-p"/> II. This general law is to be considered together with a particular law: "<hi type="italic">If you have respect to persons, you commit sin, and are convinced of the law as transgressors,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.9">v. 9</reference>. Notwithstanding the law of laws, <hi type="italic">to love your neighbour as yourselves,</hi> and to show that respect to them which you would be apt to look for yourselves if in their circumstances, yet this will not excuse your distributing either the favours or the censures of the church according to men's outward condition; but here you must look to a particular law, which God, who gave the other, has given you together with it, and by this you will stand fully convicted of the sin I have charged you with." This law is in <reference osisRef="Lev.19.15">Lev. xix. 15</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt do no unrighteousness in judgment; thou shalt not respect the person of the poor nor the person of the mighty; but in righteousness shalt though judge thy neighbour.</hi> Yea, the very royal law itself, rightly explained, would serve to convict them, because it teaches them to put themselves as much in the places of the poor as in those of the rich, and so to act equitably towards one as well as the other. Hence he proceeds, <div eID="gen33266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33267" type="x-p"/> III. To show the extent of the law, and how far obedience must be paid to it. They must fulfil the royal law, have a regard to one part as well as another, otherwise it would not stand them in stead, when they pretended to urge it as a reason for any particular actions: <hi type="italic">For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, is guilty of all,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.10">v. 10</reference>. This may be considered, 1. With reference to the case James has been upon: Do you plead for your respect to the rich, because you are to love your neighbour as yourselves? Why then show also an equitable and due regard to the poor, because you are to love your neighbour as yourself: or else your offending in one point will spoil your pretence of observing that law at all. <hi type="italic">Whosoever shall keep the whole law, if he offend in one point,</hi> wilfully, avowedly, and with continuance, and so as to think he shall be excused in some matters because of his obedience in others, <hi type="italic">he is guilty of all;</hi> that is, he incurs the same penalty, and is liable to the same punishment, by the sentence of the law, as if he had broken it in other points as well as that he stands chargeable with. Not that all sins are equal, but that all carry the same contempt of the authority of the Lawgiver, and so bind over to such punishment as is threatened on the breach of that law. This shows us what a vanity it is to think that our good deeds will atone for our bad deeds, and plainly puts us upon looking for some other atonement. 2. This is further illustrated by putting a case different from that before mentioned (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">For he that said, Do not commit adultery, said also, Do not kill. Now, if thou commit no adultery, yet, if thou kill, thou art become a transgressor of the law.</hi> One, perhaps, is very severe in the case of adultery, or what tends to such pollutions of the flesh; but less ready to condemn murder, or what tends to ruin the health, break the hearts, and destroy the lives, of others: another has a prodigious dread of murder, but has more easy thoughts of adultery; whereas one who looks at the authority of the Lawgiver more than the matter of the command will see the same reason for condemning the one as the other. Obedience is then acceptable when all is done with an eye to the will of God; and disobedience is to be condemned, in whatever instance it be, as it is a contempt of the authority of God; and, for that reason, if we offend in one point, we contemn the authority of him who gave the whole law, and so far are guilty of all. Thus, if you look to the law of the old, you stand condemned; for <hi type="italic">cursed is every that continueth not in all things that are written in the book of the law to do them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.3.10">Gal. iii. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen33267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33268" type="x-p"/> IV. James directs Christians to govern and conduct themselves more especially by the law of Christ. <hi type="italic">So speak and so do as those that shall be judged by the law of liberty,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.12">v. 12</reference>. This will teach us, not only to be just and impartial, but very compassionate and merciful to the poor; and it will set us perfectly free from all sordid and undue regards to the rich. Observe here, 1. The gospel is called a law. It has all the requisites of a law: precepts with rewards and punishments annexed; it prescribes duty, as well as administers comfort; and Christ is a king to rule us as well as a prophet to teach us, and a priest to sacrifice and intercede for us. <hi type="italic">We are under the law to Christ.</hi> 2. It is a <hi type="italic">law of liberty,</hi> and one that we have no reason to complain of as a yoke or burden; for the service of God, according to the gospel, is perfect freedom; it sets us at liberty from all slavish regards, either to the persons or the things of this world. 3. We must all be judged by this law of liberty. Men's eternal condition will be determined according to the gospel; this is the book that will be opened, when we shall stand before the judgment-seat; there will be no relief to those whom the gospel condemns, nor will any accusation lie against those whom the gospel justifies. 4. It concerns us therefore so to speak and act now as become those who must shortly be judged by this law of liberty; that is, that we come up to gospel terms, that we make conscience of gospel duties, that e be of a gospel temper, and that our conversation be a gospel conversation, because by this rule we must be judged. 5. The consideration of our being judged by the gospel should engage us more especially to be merciful in our regards to the poor (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">For he shall have judgment without mercy that hath shown no mercy; and mercy rejoiceth against judgment.</hi> Take notice here, (1.) The doom which will be passed upon impenitent sinners at last will be judgment without mercy; there will be no mixtures or allays in the cup of wrath and of trembling, the dregs of which they must drink. (2.) Such as show no mercy now shall find no mercy in the great day. But we may note, on the other hand, (3.) That there will be such as shall become instances of the triumph of mercy, in whom mercy rejoices against judgment: all the children of men, in the last day, will be either vessels of wrath or vessels of mercy. It concerns all to consider among which they shall be found; and let us remember that <hi type="italic">blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.</hi>
entries.d055c731c8db9809959b01990425afae3fd13de1: <div eID="gen33268" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Faith and Works. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 61.)</title> <div sID="gen33269" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> What <hi type="italic">doth it</hi> profit, my brethren, though a man say he hath faith, and have not works? can faith save him? <hi type="super">15</hi> If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food, <hi type="super">16</hi> And one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be <hi type="italic">ye</hi> warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what <hi type="italic">doth it</hi> profit? <hi type="super">17</hi> Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone. <hi type="super">18</hi> Yea, a man may say, Thou hast faith, and I have works: show me thy faith without thy works, and I will show thee my faith by my works. <hi type="super">19</hi> Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble. 20 But wilt thou know, O vain man, that faith without works is dead? <hi type="super">21</hi> Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he had offered Isaac his son upon the altar? <hi type="super">22</hi> Seest thou how faith wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect? <hi type="super">23</hi> And the scripture was fulfilled which saith, Abraham believed God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness: and he was called the Friend of God. <hi type="super">24</hi> Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only. <hi type="super">25</hi> Likewise also was not Rahab the harlot justified by works, when she had received the messengers, and had sent <hi type="italic">them</hi> out another way? <hi type="super">26</hi> For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also. <div eID="gen33269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33270" type="x-p"/> In this latter part of the chapter, the apostle shows the error of those who rested in a bare profession of the Christian faith, as if that would save them, while the temper of their minds and the tenour of their lives were altogether disagreeable to that holy religion which they professed. To let them see, therefore, what a wretched foundation they built their hopes upon, it is here proved at large that a man is justified, not by faith only, but by works. Now, <div eID="gen33270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33271" type="x-p"/> I. Upon this arises a very great question, namely, how to reconcile Paul and James. Paul, in his epistles to the Romans and Galatians, seems to assert the directly contrary thing to what James here lays down, saying if often, and with a great deal of emphasis, <hi type="italic">that we are justified by faith only and not by the works of the law. Amicæ scripturarum lites, utinam et nostræ—There is a very happy agreement between one part of scripture and another, notwithstanding seeming differences: it were well if the differences among Christians were as easily reconciled.</hi> "Nothing," says Mr. Baxter, "but men's misunderstanding the plain drift and sense of Paul's epistles, could make so many take it for a matter of great difficulty to reconcile Paul and James." A general view of those things which are insisted on by the Antinomians may be seen in Mr. Baxter's Paraphrase: and many ways might be mentioned which have been invented among learned men to make the apostles agree; but it may be sufficient only to observe these few things following:—1. When Paul says that <hi type="italic">a man is justified by faith, without the deeds of the law</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.28">Rom. iii. 28</reference>), he plainly speaks of another sort of work than James does, but not of another sort of faith. Paul speaks of works wrought in obedience to the law of Moses, and before men's embracing the faith of the gospel; and he had to deal with those who valued themselves so highly upon those works that they rejected the gospel (as <reference osisRef="Rom.10.1-Rom.10.21">Rom. x.</reference>, at the beginning most expressly declares); but James speaks of works done in obedience to the gospel, and as the proper and necessary effects and fruits of sound believing in Christ Jesus. Both are concerned to magnify the faith of the gospel, as that which alone could save us and justify us; but Paul magnifies it by showing the insufficiency of any works of the law before faith, or in opposition to the doctrine of justification by Jesus Christ; James magnifies the same faith, by showing what are the genuine and necessary products and operations of it. 2. Paul not only speaks of different works from those insisted on by James, but he speaks of a quite different use that was made of good works from what is here urged and intended. Paul had to do with those who depended on the merit of their works in the sight of God, and thus he might well make them of no manner of account. James had to do with those who cried up faith, but would not allow works to be used even as evidence; they depended upon a bare profession, as sufficient to justify them; and with these he might well urge the necessity and vast importance of good works. As we must not break one table of the law, by dashing it against the other, so neither must we break in pieces the law and the gospel, by making them clash with one another: those who cry up the gospel so as to set aside the law, and those who cry up the law so as to set aside the gospel, are both in the wrong; for we must take our work before us; there must be both faith in Jesus Christ and good works the fruit of faith. 3. The justification of which Paul speaks is different from that spoken of by James; the one speaks of our persons being justified before God, the other speaks of our faith being justified before men: "<hi type="italic">Show me thy faith by thy works,</hi>" says James, "let thy faith be justified in the eyes of those that behold thee by thy works;" but Paul speaks of justification in the sight of God, who justifies those only that believe in Jesus, and purely on account of the redemption that is in him. Thus we see that our persons are justified before God by faith, but our faith is justified before men by works. This is so plainly the scope and design of the apostle James that he is but confirming what Paul, in other places, says of his faith, that it is a laborious faith, and a faith working by love, <reference osisRef="Gal.5.6">Gal. v. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.3">1 Thess. i. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.3.8">Titus iii. 8</reference>; and many other places. 4. Paul may be understood as speaking of that justification which is inchoate, James of that which is complete; it is by <hi type="italic">faith</hi> only that we are put into a justified state, but then good works come in for the completing of our justification at the last great day; then, <hi type="italic">Come you children of my Father—for I was hungry, and you gave me meat,</hi> &c. <div eID="gen33271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33272" type="x-p"/> II. Having thus cleared this part of scripture from every thing of a contradiction to other parts of it, let us see what is more particularly to be learnt from this excellent passage of James; we are taught, <div eID="gen33272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33273" type="x-p"/> 1. That faith without works will not profit, and cannot save us. <hi type="italic">What doth it profit, my brethren, if a man say he hath faith, and have not works? Can faith save him?</hi> Observe here, (1.) That faith which does not save will not really profit us; a bare profession may sometimes seem to be profitable, to gain the good opinion of those who are truly good, and it may procure in some cases worldly good things; but what profit will this be, for any to gain the world and to lose their souls? <hi type="italic">What doth it profit?—Can faith save him?</hi> All things should be accounted profitable or unprofitable to us as they tend to forward or hinder the salvation of our souls. And, above all other things, we should take care thus to make account of faith, as that which does not profit, if it do not save, but will aggravate our condemnation and destruction at last. (2.) For a man to have faith, and to say he has faith, are two different things; the apostle does not say, <hi type="italic">If a man have faith without works,</hi> for that is not a supposable case; the drift of this place of scripture is plainly to show that an opinion, or speculation, or assent, without works, is not faith; but the case is put thus, <hi type="italic">If a man say he hath faith,</hi> &c. Men may boast of that to others, and be conceited of that in themselves, of which they are really destitute. <div eID="gen33273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33274" type="x-p"/> 2. We are taught that, as love or charity is an operative principle, so is faith, and that neither of them would otherwise be good for any thing; and, by trying how it looks for a person to pretend he is very charitable who yet never does any works of charity, you may judge what sense there is in pretending to have faith without the proper and necessary fruits of it: "<hi type="italic">If a brother or a sister be naked, and destitute of daily food, and one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be you warmed and filled, notwithstanding you give them not those things which are needful to the body, what doth it profit?</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.15-Jas.2.17">v. 15-17</reference>. What will such a charity as this, that consists in bare words, avail either you or the poor? Will you come before God with such empty shows of charity as these? You might as well pretend that your love and charity will stand the test without acts of mercy as think that a profession of faith will bear you out before God without works of piety and obedience. <hi type="italic">Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being along,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Jas.2.17">v. 17</reference>. We are too apt to rest in a bare profession of faith, and to think that this will save us; it is a cheap and easy religion to say, "We believe the articles of the Christian faith;" but it is a great delusion to imagine that this is enough to bring us to heaven. Those who argue thus wrong God, and put a cheat upon their own souls; a mock-faith is as hateful as mock-charity, and both show a heart dead to all real godliness. You may as soon take pleasure in a dead body, void of soul, or sense, or action, as God take pleasure in a dead faith, where there are no works. <div eID="gen33274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33275" type="x-p"/> 3. We are taught to compare a faith boasting of itself without works and a faith evidenced by works, by looking on both together, to try how this comparison will work upon our minds. <hi type="italic">Yea, a man may say, Thou hast faith, and I have works. Show me thy faith without thy works, and I will show thee my faith by my works,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.18">v. 18</reference>. Suppose a true believer thus pleading with a boasting hypocrite, "Thou makest a profession, and sayest thou hast faith; I make no such boasts, but leave my works to speak for me. Now give any evidence of having the faith thou professest without works if thou canst, and I will soon let thee see how my works flow from faith and are the undoubted evidences of its existence." This is the evidence by which the scriptures all along teach men to judge both of themselves and others. And this is the evidence according to which Christ will proceed at the day of judgment. <hi type="italic">The dead were judged according to their works,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.20.12">Rev. xx. 12</reference>. How will those be exposed then who boast of that which they cannot evidence, or who go about to evidence their faith by any thing but works of piety and mercy! <div eID="gen33275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33276" type="x-p"/> 4. We are taught to look upon a faith of bare speculation and knowledge as the faith of devils: <hi type="italic">Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well; the devils also believe, and tremble,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.19">v. 19</reference>. That instance of faith which the apostle here chooses to mention is the first principle of all religion. "<hi type="italic">Thou believest that there is a God,</hi> against the atheists; and that there is but one God, against the idolaters; <hi type="italic">thou doest well:</hi> so far all is right. But to rest here, and take up a good opinion of thyself, or of thy state towards God, merely on account of thy believing in him, this will render thee miserable: <hi type="italic">The devils also believe, and tremble.</hi> If thou contentest thyself with a bare assent to articles of faith, and some speculations upon them, thus far the devils go. And as their faith and knowledge only serve to excite horror, so in a little time will thine." The word tremble is commonly looked upon as denoting a good effect of faith; but here it may rather be taken as a bad effect, when applied to the faith of devils. They tremble, not out of reverence, but hatred and opposition to that one God on whom they believe. To rehearse that article of our creed, therefore, <hi type="italic">I believe in God the Father Almighty,</hi> will not distinguish us from devils at last, unless we now give up ourselves to God as the gospel directs, and love him, and delight ourselves in him, and serve him, which the devils do not, cannot do. <div eID="gen33276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33277" type="x-p"/> 5. We are taught that he who boasts of faith without works is to be looked upon at present as a foolish condemned person. <hi type="italic">But wilt thou know, O vain man, that faith without works is dead?</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.20">v. 20</reference>. The words translated <hi type="italic">vain man</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">anthrope kene,</hi></hi> are observed to have the same signification with the word <hi type="italic">Raca,</hi> which must never be used to private persons, or as an effect of anger (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.22">Matt. v. 22</reference>), but may be used as here, to denote a just detestation of such a sort of men as are empty of good works, and yet boasters of their faith. And it plainly declares them fools and abjects in the sight of God. Faith without works is said to be <hi type="italic">dead,</hi> not only as void of all those operations which are the proofs of spiritual life, but as unavailable to eternal life: such believers as rest in a bare profession of faith <hi type="italic">are dead while they live.</hi> <div eID="gen33277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33278" type="x-p"/> 6. We are taught that a justifying faith cannot be without works, from two examples, Abraham and Rahab. <div eID="gen33278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33279" type="x-p"/> (1.) The first instance is that of Abraham, the father of the faithful, and the prime example of justification, to whom the Jews had a special regard (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he had offered Isaac his son upon the altar?</hi> Paul, on the other hand, says (in <reference osisRef="Rom.4.3">ch. 4 of the epistle to the Romans</reference>) that Abraham <hi type="italic">believed, and it was counted to him for righteousness.</hi> But these are well reconciled, by observing what is said in <reference osisRef="Heb.11.1-Heb.11.40">Heb. 11</reference>, which shows that the faith both of Abraham and Rahab was such as to produce those good works of which James speaks, and which are not to be separated from faith as justifying and saving. By what Abraham did, it appeared that he truly believed. Upon this footing, the words of God himself plainly put this matter. <reference osisRef="Gen.22.16-Gen.22.17">Gen. xxii. 16, 17</reference>, <hi type="italic">Because thou hast done this thing, and hast not withheld thy son, thine only son; therefore in blessing I will bless thee.</hi> Thus the faith of Abraham was a working faith (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.22">v. 22</reference>), <hi type="italic">it wrought with his works, and by works was made perfect.</hi> And by this means you come to the true sense of that scripture which saith, Abraham believed God, <hi type="italic">and it was imputed unto him for righteousness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.23">v. 23</reference>. And thus he became the <hi type="italic">friend of God.</hi> Faith, producing such works, endeared him to the divine Being, and advanced him to very peculiar favours and intimacies with God. It is a great honour done to Abraham that he is called and counted the friend of God. You see then (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.24">v. 24</reference>) how that <hi type="italic">by works a man is justified</hi> (comes into such a state of favour and friendship with God), <hi type="italic">and not by faith only;</hi> not by a bare opinion, or profession, or believing without obeying, but by having such a faith as is productive of good works. Now besides the explication of this passage and example, as thus illustrating and supporting the argument James is upon, many other useful lessons may be learned by us from what is here said concerning Abraham. [1.] Those who would have Abraham's blessings must be careful to copy after his faith: to boast of being Abraham's seed will not avail any, if they do not believe as he did. [2.] Those works which evidence true faith must to works of self-denial, and such as God himself commands (as Abraham's offering up his son, his only son, was), and not such works as are pleasing to flesh and blood and may serve our interest, or are the mere fruits of our own imagination and devising. [3.] What we piously purpose and sincerely resolve to do for God is accepted as if actually performed. Thus Abraham is regarded as offering up his son, though he did not actually proceed to make a sacrifice of him. It was a done thing in the mind, and spirit, and resolution of Abraham, and God accepts it as if fully performed and accomplished. [4.] The actings of faith make it grow perfect, as the truth of faith makes it act. [5.] Such an acting faith will make others, as well as Abraham, friends of God. Thus Christ says to his disciples, <hi type="italic">I have called you friends,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.15.15">John xv. 15</reference>. All transactions between God and the truly believing soul are easy, pleasant, and delightful. There is one will and one heart, and there is a mutual complacency. <hi type="italic">God rejoiceth over those</hi> who truly believe, to do them good; and they delight themselves in him. <div eID="gen33279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33280" type="x-p"/> (2.) The second example of faith's justifying itself and us with and by works is Rahab: <hi type="italic">Likewise also was not Rahab the harlot justified by works, when she had received the messengers, and had sent them out another way?</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.25">v. 25</reference>. The former instance was of one renowned for his faith all his life long, This is of one noted for sin, whose faith was meaner and of a much lower degree; so that the strongest faith will not do, nor the meanest be allowed to go without works. Some say that the word here rendered <hi type="italic">harlot</hi> was the proper name of Rahab. Others tell us that it signifies no more than a <hi type="italic">hostess,</hi> or one who keeps a public house, with whom therefore the spies lodged. But it is very probable that her character was infamous; and such an instance is mentioned to show that faith will save the worst, when evidenced by proper works; and it will not save the best without such works as God requires. This Rahab believed the report she had heard of God's powerful presence with Israel; but that which proved her faith sincere was, that, to the hazard of her life, she <hi type="italic">received the messengers, and sent them out another way.</hi> Observe here, [1.] The wonderful power of faith in transforming and changing sinners. [2.] The regard which an operative faith meets with from God, to obtain his mercy and favour. [3.] Where great sins are pardoned, there must prefer the honour of God and the good of his people before the preservation of her own country. Her former acquaintance must be discarded, her former course of life entirely abandoned, and she must give signal proof and evidence of this before she can be in a justified state; and even after she is justified, yet her former character must be remembered; not so much to her dishonour as to glorify the rich grace and mercy of God. Though justified, she is called <hi type="italic">Rahab the harlot.</hi> <div eID="gen33280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33281" type="x-p"/> 7. And now, upon the whole matter, the apostle draws this conclusion, <hi type="italic">As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.26">v. 26</reference>. These words are read differently; some reading them, <hi type="italic">As the body without the breath is dead, so is faith without works:</hi> and then they show that works are the companions of faith, as breathing is of life. Others read them, <hi type="italic">As the body without the soul is dead, so faith without works is dead also:</hi> and then they show that as the body has no action, nor beauty, but becomes a loathsome carcass, when the soul is gone, so a bare profession without works is useless, yea, loathsome and offensive. Let us then take head of running into extremes in this case. For, (1.) The best works, without faith, are dead; they want their root and principle. It is by faith that any thing we do is really good, as done with an eye to God, in obedience to him, and so as to aim principally at his acceptance. (2.) The most plausible profession of faith, without works, is dead: as the root is dead when it produces nothing green, nothing of fruit. Faith is the root, good works are the fruits, and we must see to it that we have both. We must not think that either, without the other, will justify and save us. This is the grace of God wherein we stand, and we should stand to it.  <chapter eID="Jas.2"/> <div eID="gen33281" type="x-p"/>

entries.150f3fcccd9710ca524d8cc4c71c744fff73c07e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18647"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jas.2.1-Jas.2.26">Jas 2:1-26</reference>. The Sin of Respect of Persons: Dead, Unworking Faith Saves No Man.</title> <div sID="gen39459" type="x-p"/> James illustrates "the perfect law of liberty" (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.25">Jas 1:25</reference>) in one particular instance of a sin against it, concluding with a reference again to that law (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.12">Jas 2:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.13">13</reference>).<div eID="gen39459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39460" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18647"/><hi type="bold">1. brethren--</hi>The equality of all Christians as "brethren," forms the groundwork of the admonition.<div eID="gen39460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39461" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the faith of ... Christ--</hi>that is, the Christian faith. James grounds Christian practice on Christian faith.<div eID="gen39461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39462" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord of glory--</hi>So <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">1Co 2:8</reference>. As all believers, alike rich and poor, derive all their glory from their union with Him, "the Lord of glory," not from external advantages of worldly fortune, the sin in question is peculiarly inconsistent with His "faith." Bengel, making no ellipsis of "the Lord," explains "glory" as in apposition with Christ who is THE GLORY (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.32">Lu 2:32</reference>); the true Shekinah glory of the temple (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.4">Ro 9:4</reference>). English Version is simpler. The glory of Christ resting on the poor believer should make him be regarded as highly by "brethren" as his richer brother; nay, more so, if the poor believer has more of Christ's spirit than the rich brother.<div eID="gen39462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39463" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with respect of persons--</hi>literally, "in respectings of persons"; "in" the practice of partial preferences of persons in various ways and on various occasions. <div eID="gen39463" type="x-p"/>
entries.d76bac4d6100e898e0f6e14fcf79c6b08c8702d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18648"/><div sID="gen39464" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18648"/>2-3. "If there chance to have come" [Alford].<div eID="gen39464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39465" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">assembly--</hi>literally, "synagogue"; this, the latest honorable use, and the only Christian use of the term in the New Testament, occurs in James's Epistle, the apostle who maintained to the latest possible moment the bonds between the Jewish synagogue and the Christian Church. Soon the continued resistance of the truth by the Jews led Christians to leave the term to them exclusively (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.9">Re 3:9</reference>). The "synagogue" implies a mere assembly or congregation not necessarily united by any common tie. "Church," a people bound together by mutual ties and laws, though often it may happen that the members are not assembled [Trench and Vitringa]. Partly from James' Hebrew tendencies, partly from the Jewish Christian churches retaining most of the Jewish forms, this term "synagogue" is used here instead of the Christian term "Church" (ecclesia, derived from a root, "called out," implying the union of its members in spiritual bonds, independent of space, and called out into separation from the world); an undesigned coincidence and mark of truth. The people in the Jewish synagogue sat according to their rank, those of the same trade together. The introduction of this custom into Jewish Christian places of worship is here reprobated by James. Christian churches were built like the synagogues, the holy table in the east end of the former, as the ark was in the latter; the desk and pulpit were the chief articles of furniture in both alike. This shows the error of comparing the Church to the temple, and the ministry to the priesthood; the temple is represented by the whole body of worshippers; the church building was formed on the model of the synagogue. See Vitringa [Synagogue and Temple].<div eID="gen39465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39466" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">goodly apparel ... gay clothing--</hi>As the Greek, is the same in both, translate both alike, "gay," or "splendid clothing." <div eID="gen39466" type="x-p"/>
entries.0e28672377681d3b77435b82b5854f9876d41ace: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18650"/><div sID="gen39472" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18650"/><hi type="bold">4. Are ye not ... partial--</hi>literally, "Have ye not made distinctions" or "differences" (so as to prefer one to another)? So in Jude 22.<div eID="gen39472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39473" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in yourselves--</hi>in your minds, that is, according to your carnal inclination [Grotius].<div eID="gen39473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39474" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are become judges of evil thoughts--</hi>The Greek words for "judges" and for "partial," are akin in sound and meaning. A similar translation ought therefore to be given to both. Thus, either for "judges," &c. translate, "distinguishers of (that is, according to your) evil thoughts"; or, do ye not partially judge between men, and are become evilly-thinking judges (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.21">Mr 7:21</reference>)? The "evil thoughts" are in the judges themselves; as in <reference osisRef="Luke.18.6">Lu 18:6</reference>, the Greek, "judge of injustice," is translated, "unjust judge." Alford and Wahl translate, "Did ye not doubt" (respecting your faith, which is inconsistent with the distinctions made by you between rich and poor)? For the Greek constantly means "doubt" in all the New Testament. So in <reference osisRef="Jas.1.6">Jas 1:6</reference>, "wavering." <reference osisRef="Matt.21.21">Mt 21:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.10.20">Ac 10:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.4.20">Ro 4:20</reference>, "staggered not." The same play on the same kindred words occurs in the Greek of <reference osisRef="Rom.14.10">Ro 14:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.14.23">23</reference>, "judge ... doubteth." The same blame of being a judge, when one ought to be an obeyer, of the law is found in <reference osisRef="Jas.4.11">Jas 4:11</reference>. <div eID="gen39474" type="x-p"/>
entries.24ff0ab79d4b4417bea73cfbfbbd7d481f301b2a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18651"/><div sID="gen39475" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18651"/><hi type="bold">5. Hearken--</hi>James brings to trial the self-constituted "judges" (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.4">Jas 2:4</reference>).<div eID="gen39475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39476" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">poor of this world--</hi>The best manuscripts read, "those poor in respect to the world." In contrast to "the rich in this world" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.17">1Ti 6:17</reference>). Not of course all the poor; but the poor, as a class, furnish more believers than the rich as a class. The rich, if a believer, renounces riches as his portion; the poor, if an unbeliever, neglects that which is the peculiar advantage of poverty (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.3">Mt 5:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.26">1Co 1:26</reference>, 27, 28).<div eID="gen39476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39477" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rich in faith--</hi>Their riches consist in faith. <reference osisRef="Luke.12.21">Lu 12:21</reference>, "rich toward God." <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.18">1Ti 6:18</reference>, "rich in good works" (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.9">Re 2:9</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.9">2Co 8:9</reference>). Christ's poverty is the source of the believer's riches.<div eID="gen39477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39478" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kingdom ... promised--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Luke.12.32">Lu 12:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.9">1Co 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.8">2Ti 4:8</reference>). <div eID="gen39478" type="x-p"/>
entries.5e141724852ed6dfff410154f40d1e4be9f32d41: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18652"/><div sID="gen39479" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18652"/>6. The world's judgment of the poor contrasted with God's.<div eID="gen39479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39480" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye--</hi>Christians, from whom better things might have been expected; there is no marvel that men of the world do so.<div eID="gen39480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39481" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">despised--</hi>literally, "dishonored." To dishonor the poor is to dishonor those whom God honors, and so to invert the order of God [Calvin].<div eID="gen39481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39482" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rich--</hi>as a class.<div eID="gen39482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39483" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">oppress--</hi>literally, "abuse their power against" you.<div eID="gen39483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39484" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">draw you--</hi>Translate, "is it not they (those very persons whom ye partially prefer, <reference osisRef="Jas.2.1-Jas.2.4">Jas 2:1-4</reference>) that drag you (namely, with violence)" [Alford].<div eID="gen39484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39485" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before ... judgment seats--</hi>instituting persecutions for religion, as well as oppressive lawsuits, against you. <div eID="gen39485" type="x-p"/>
entries.8bb0615d3086aa4dba2d145aa09acca35c7976a0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18653"/><div sID="gen39486" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18653"/>7. "Is it not they that blaspheme?" &c. as in <reference osisRef="Jas.2.6">Jas 2:6</reference> [Alford]. Rich heathen must here chiefly be meant; for none others would directly blaspheme the name of Christ. Only indirectly rich Christians can be meant, who, by their inconsistency, caused His name to be blasphemed; so <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.21">Eze 36:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.22">22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.2.24">Ro 2:24</reference>. Besides, there were few rich Jewish Christians at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.26">Ro 15:26</reference>). They who dishonor God's name by wilful and habitual sin, "take (or bear) the Lord's name in vain" (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.30.9">Pr 30:9</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Exod.20.7">Ex 20:7</reference>).<div eID="gen39486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39487" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that worthy name--</hi>which is "good before the Lord's saints" (<reference osisRef="Ps.52.9">Psa 52:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.54.6">54:6</reference>); which ye pray may be "hallowed" (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.9">Mt 6:9</reference>), and "by which ye are called," literally, "which was invoked" or, "called upon by you" (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.48.16">Ge 48:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.4.1">Is 4:1</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Acts.15.17">Ac 15:17</reference>), so that at your baptism "into the name" (so the Greek, <reference osisRef="Matt.28.19">Mt 28:19</reference>) of Christ, ye became Christ's people (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.23">1Co 3:23</reference>). <div eID="gen39487" type="x-p"/>
entries.184a016f502f2b8dc72d3c38c1778d6f6ec16e56: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18654"/><div sID="gen39488" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18654"/>8. The Greek may be translated, "If, however, ye fulfil," &c., that is, as Alford, after Estius, explains, "Still I do not say, hate the rich (for their oppressions) and drive them from your assemblies; if you choose to observe the royal law ... well and good; but respect of persons is a breach of that law." I think the translation is, "If in very deed (or 'indeed on the one hand') ye fulfil the royal law ... ye do well, but if (on the other hand) ye respect persons, ye practice sin." The Jewish Christians boasted of, and rested in, the "law" (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.1">Ac 15:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.21.18-Acts.21.24">21:18-24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.2.17">Ro 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.2.12">Ga 2:12</reference>). To this the "indeed" alludes. "(Ye rest in the law): If indeed (then) ye fulfil it, ye do well; but if," &c.<div eID="gen39488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39489" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">royal--</hi>the law that is king of all laws, being the sum and essence of the ten commandments. The great King, God, is love; His law is the royal law of love, and that law, like Himself, reigns supreme. He "is no respecter of persons"; therefore to respect persons is at variance with Him and His royal law, which is at once a law of love and of liberty (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.12">Jas 2:12</reference>). The law is the "whole"; "the (particular) Scripture" (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.18">Le 19:18</reference>) quoted is a part. To break a part is to break the whole (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.10">Jas 2:10</reference>).<div eID="gen39489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39490" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye do well--</hi>being "blessed in your deed" ("doing," Margin) as a doer, not a forgetful hearer of the law (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.25">Jas 1:25</reference>). <div eID="gen39490" type="x-p"/>
entries.5e529a0fd7415c48dd44c089e303e3e5e8a5ed1b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18655"/><div sID="gen39491" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18655"/>9. Respect of persons violates the command to love all alike "as thyself."<div eID="gen39491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39492" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye commit sin--</hi>literally, "ye work sin," <reference osisRef="Matt.7.23">Mt 7:23</reference>, to which the reference here is probably, as in <reference osisRef="Jas.1.22">Jas 1:22</reference>. Your works are sin, whatever boast of the law ye make in words (see on <reference osisRef="Jas.2.8">Jas 2:8</reference>).<div eID="gen39492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39493" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">convinced--</hi>Old English for "convicted."<div eID="gen39493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39494" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as transgressors--</hi>not merely of this or that particular command, but of the whole absolutely. <div eID="gen39494" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf830949c329608f7c6a8a15776ba352c8b1eb1d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18656"/><div sID="gen39495" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18656"/>10. The best manuscripts read, "Whosoever shall have kept the whole law, and yet shall have offended (literally, 'stumbled'; not so strong as 'fall,' <reference osisRef="Rom.11.11">Ro 11:11</reference>) in one (point; here, the respecting of persons), is (hereby) become guilty of all." The law is one seamless garment which is rent if you but rend a part; or a musical harmony which is spoiled if there be one discordant note [Tirinus]; or a golden chain whose completeness is broken if you break one link [Gataker]. You thus break the whole law, though not the whole of the law, because you offend against love, which is the fulfilling of the law. If any part of a man be leprous, the whole man is judged to be a leper. God requires perfect, not partial, obedience. We are not to choose out parts of the law to keep, which suit our whim, while we neglect others. <div eID="gen39495" type="x-p"/>
entries.2441aa8ca52bb1c1881875e1af267e3c4a535110: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18657"/><div sID="gen39496" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18657"/>11. He is One who gave the whole law; therefore, they who violate His will in one point, violate it all [Bengel]. The law and its Author alike have a complete unity.<div eID="gen39496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39497" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">adultery ... kill--</hi>selected as being the most glaring cases of violation of duty towards one's neighbor. <div eID="gen39497" type="x-p"/>
entries.5d12e1435e3fe26c18df7517d55efa6f3bd737a5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18658"/><div sID="gen39498" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18658"/>12. Summing up of the previous reasonings.<div eID="gen39498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39499" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">speak--</hi>referring back to <reference osisRef="Jas.1.19">Jas 1:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.26">26</reference>; the fuller discussion of the topic is given <reference osisRef="Jas.3.5-Jas.3.12">Jas 3:5-12</reference>.<div eID="gen39499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39500" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judged by the law of liberty--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jas.1.25">Jas 1:25</reference>); that is, the Gospel law of love, which is not a law of external constraint, but of internal, free, instinctive inclination. The law of liberty, through God's mercy, frees us from the curse of the law, that henceforth we should be free to love and obey willingly. If we will not in turn practice the law of love to our neighbor, that law of grace condemns us still more heavily than the old law, which spake nothing but wrath to him who offended in the least particular (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.13">Jas 2:13</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Matt.18.32-Matt.18.35">Mt 18:32-35</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.48">Joh 12:48</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.6.16">Re 6:16</reference>, "Wrath of the (merciful) Lamb." <div eID="gen39500" type="x-p"/>
entries.bf4eb6dac16f284312771b81ad59c37aa6cef3c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18659"/><div sID="gen39501" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18659"/>13. The converse of, "Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy" (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.7">Mt 5:7</reference>). Translate, "The judgment (which is coming on all of us) shall be without mercy to him who hath showed no mercy." It shall be such toward every one as every one shall have been [Bengel]. "Mercy" here corresponds to "love," <reference osisRef="Jas.2.8">Jas 2:8</reference>.<div eID="gen39501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39502" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mercy rejoiceth against judgment--</hi>Mercy, so far from fearing judgment in the case of its followers, actually glorifieth against it, knowing that it cannot condemn them. Not that their mercy is the ground of their acquittal, but the mercy of God in Christ towards them, producing mercy on their part towards their fellow men, makes them to triumph over judgment, which all in themselves otherwise deserve. <div eID="gen39502" type="x-p"/>
entries.d4f3800dd74ce14ff748fc77b1bdf7e403da2320: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18660"/><div sID="gen39503" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18660"/>14. James here, passing from the particular case of "mercy" or "love" violated by "respect of persons," notwithstanding profession of the "faith of our Lord Jesus" (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.1">Jas 2:1</reference>), combats the Jewish tendency (transplanted into their Christianity) to substitute a lifeless, inoperative acquaintance with the letter of the law, for change of heart to practical holiness, as if justification could be thereby attained (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.3">Ro 2:3</reference>, 13, 23). It seems hardly likely but that James had seen Paul's Epistles, considering that he uses the same phrases and examples (compare <reference osisRef="Jas.2.21">Jas 2:21</reference>, 23, 25, with <reference osisRef="Rom.4.3">Ro 4:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.17">He 11:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.31">31</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Jas.2.14">Jas 2:14</reference>, 24, with <reference osisRef="Rom.3.28">Ro 3:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.2.16">Ga 2:16</reference>). Whether James individually designed it or not, the Holy Spirit by him combats not Paul, but those who abuse Paul's doctrine. The teaching of both alike is inspired, and is therefore to be received without wresting of words; but each has a different class to deal with; Paul, self-justiciaries; James, Antinomian advocates of a mere notional faith. Paul urged as strongly as James the need of works as evidences of faith, especially in the later Epistles, when many were abusing the doctrine of faith (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.14">Tit 2:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.8">3:8</reference>). "Believing and doing are blood relatives" [Rutherford].<div eID="gen39503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39504" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">What doth it profit--</hi>literally, "What is the profit?"<div eID="gen39504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39505" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">though a man say--</hi>James' expression is not, "If a man have faith," but "if a man say he hath faith"; referring to a mere profession of faith, such as was usually made at baptism. Simon Magus so "believed and was baptized," and yet had "neither part nor lot in this matter," for his "heart," as his words and works evinced, was not right in the sight of God. Alford wrongly denies that "say" is emphatic. The illustration, <reference osisRef="Jas.2.16">Jas 2:16</reference>, proves it is: "If one of you say" to a naked brother, "Be ye warmed, notwithstanding ye give not those things needful." The inoperative profession of sympathy answering to the inoperative profession of faith.<div eID="gen39505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39506" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">can faith save him--</hi>rather, "can such a faith (literally, 'the faith') save him?"--the faith you pretend to: the empty name of boasted faith, contrasted with true fruit-producing faith. So that which self-deceivers claim is called "wisdom," though not true wisdom, <reference osisRef="Jas.3.15">Jas 3:15</reference>. The "him" also in the Greek is emphatic; the particular man who professes faith without having the works which evidence its vitality. <div eID="gen39506" type="x-p"/>
entries.281245de370e5f4e78d4c8b4d3fe61b0557602c1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18661"/><div sID="gen39507" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18661"/>15. The Greek is, "But if," &c.: the "But" taking up the argument against such a one as "said he had faith, and yet had not works," which are its fruits.<div eID="gen39507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39508" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a brother, &c.--</hi>a fellow Christian, to whom we are specially bound to give help, independent of our general obligation to help all our fellow creatures.<div eID="gen39508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39509" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be--</hi>The Greek implies, "be found, on your access to them." <div eID="gen39509" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c3adec910c7b40c3d820e0a8f10bdc9f3faf9cf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18662"/><div sID="gen39510" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18662"/>16. The habit of receiving passively sentimental impressions from sights of woe without carrying them out into active habits only hardens the heart.<div eID="gen39510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39511" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one of you--</hi>James brings home the case to his hearers individually.<div eID="gen39511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39512" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Depart in peace--</hi>as if all their wants were satisfied by the mere words addressed to them. The same words in the mouth of Christ, whose faith they said they had, were accompanied by efficient deeds of love.<div eID="gen39512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39513" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be ... warmed--</hi>with clothing, instead of being as heretofore "naked" (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.15">Jas 2:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.20">Job 31:20</reference>).<div eID="gen39513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39514" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">filled--</hi>instead of being "destitute of food" (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.37">Mt 15:37</reference>).<div eID="gen39514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39515" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what doth it profit--</hi>concluding with the same question as at the beginning, <reference osisRef="Jas.2.14">Jas 2:14</reference>. Just retribution: kind professions unaccompanied with corresponding acts, as they are of no "profit" to the needy object of them, so are of no profit to the professor himself. So faith consisting in mere profession is unacceptable to God, the object of faith, and profitless to the possessor. <div eID="gen39515" type="x-p"/>
entries.9e099d86242bd885187800469de4bed25fdb071b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18663"/><div sID="gen39516" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18663"/><hi type="bold">17. faith ... being alone--</hi>Alford joins "is dead in itself." So Bengel, "If the works which living faith produces have no existence, it is a proof that faith itself (literally, 'in respect to itself') has no existence; that is, that what one boasts of as faith, is dead." "Faith" is said to be "dead in itself," because when it has works it is alive, and it is discerned to be so, not in respect to its works, but in respect to itself. English Version, if retained, must not be understood to mean that faith can exist "alone" (that is, severed from works), but thus: Even so presumed faith, if it have not works, is dead, being by itself "alone," that is, severed from works of charity; just as the body would be "dead" if alone, that is, severed from the spirit (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.26">Jas 2:26</reference>). So Estius. <div eID="gen39516" type="x-p"/>
entries.9733c2d14d3b4cfbd7488373651b10064ba8a6c9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18664"/><div sID="gen39517" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18664"/>18. "But some one will say": so the Greek. This verse continues the argument from <reference osisRef="Jas.2.14">Jas 2:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.16">16</reference>. One may say he has faith though he have not works. Suppose one were to say to a naked brother, "Be warmed," without giving him needful clothing. "But someone (entertaining views of the need of faith having works joined to it) will say (in opposition to the 'say' of the professor)."<div eID="gen39517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39518" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">show me thy faith without thy works--</hi>if thou canst; but thou canst not SHOW, that is, manifest or evidence thy alleged (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.14">Jas 2:14</reference>, "say") faith without works. "Show" does not mean here to prove to me, but exhibit to me. Faith is unseen save by God. To show faith to man, works in some form or other are needed: we are justified judicially by God (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.33">Ro 8:33</reference>); meritoriously, by Christ (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">Is 53:11</reference>); mediately, by faith (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.1">Ro 5:1</reference>); evidentially, by works. The question here is not as to the ground on which believers are justified, but about the demonstration of their faith: so in the case of Abraham. In <reference osisRef="Gen.22.1">Ge 22:1</reference> it is written, God did tempt Abraham, that is, put to the test of demonstration the reality of his faith, not for the satisfaction of God, who already knew it well, but to demonstrate it before men. The offering of Isaac at that time, quoted here, <reference osisRef="Jas.2.21">Jas 2:21</reference>, formed no part of the ground of his justification, for he was justified previously on his simply believing in the promise of spiritual heirs, that is, believers, numerous as the stars. He was then justified: that justification was showed or manifested by his offering Isaac forty years after. That work of faith demonstrated, but did not contribute to his justification. The tree shows its life by its fruits, but it was alive before either fruits or even leaves appeared. <div eID="gen39518" type="x-p"/>
entries.e8f1bb9ab246ed533e7a4ea714643b546c080d82: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18665"/><div sID="gen39519" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18665"/><hi type="bold">19. Thou--</hi>emphatic. Thou self-deceiving claimant to faith without works.<div eID="gen39519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39520" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that there is one God--</hi>rather, "that God is one": God's existence, however, is also asserted. The fundamental article of the creed of Jews and Christians alike, and the point of faith on which especially the former boasted themselves, as distinguishing them from the Gentiles, and hence adduced by James here.<div eID="gen39520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39521" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou doest well--</hi>so far good. But unless thy faith goes farther than an assent to this truth, "the evil spirits (literally, 'demons': 'devil' is the term restricted to Satan, their head) believe" so far in common with thee, "and (so far from being saved by such a faith) shudder (so the Greek)," <reference osisRef="Matt.8.29">Mt 8:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.4.34">Lu 4:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.4">2Pe 2:4</reference>; Jude 6; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.10">Re 20:10</reference>. Their faith only adds to their torment at the thought of having to meet Him who is to consign them to their just doom: so thine (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.26">He 10:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.27">27</reference>, it is not the faith of love, but of fear, that hath torment, <reference osisRef="1John.4.18">1Jo 4:18</reference>). <div eID="gen39521" type="x-p"/>
entries.b4648091d08eb7575dc8560310053e2e2afc86a3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18666"/><div sID="gen39522" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18666"/><hi type="bold">20. wilt thou know--</hi>"Vain" men are not willing to know, since they have no wish to "do" the will of God. James beseeches such a one to lay aside his perverse unwillingness to know what is palpable to all who are willing to do.<div eID="gen39522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39523" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vain--</hi>who deceivest thyself with a delusive hope, resting on an unreal faith.<div eID="gen39523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39524" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without works--</hi>The Greek, implies separate from the works [Alford] which ought to flow from it if it were real.<div eID="gen39524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39525" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is dead--</hi>Some of the best manuscripts read, "is idle," that is, unavailing to effect what you hope, namely, to save you. <div eID="gen39525" type="x-p"/>
entries.bae9be14c47119e1610025b65d48a7741d66a5b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18667"/><div sID="gen39526" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18667"/><hi type="bold">21. Abraham ... justified by works--</hi>evidentially, and before men (see on <reference osisRef="Jas.2.18">Jas 2:18</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Jas.2.23">Jas 2:23</reference>, James, like Paul, recognizes the Scripture truth, that it was his faith that was counted to Abraham for righteousness in his justification before God.<div eID="gen39526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39527" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when he had offered--</hi>rather, "when he offered" [Alford], that is, brought as an offering at the altar; not implying that he actually offered him. <div eID="gen39527" type="x-p"/>
