                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:575" />16 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Joh. 3.18.</ns0:note> one of you say unto them, De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />part in peace <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">An usual form of Salutation, wherein, under the name of peace, they wished all Prosperity and Happiness to them they greet<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 5.34. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 7.50. and 8.48.</ns0:note>, be ye warmed <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">i. e. Be ye clothed; the Warmth here mentioned being such as is procured by Cloathes, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 31.20.</ns0:note>, and be ye filled <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>satisfied</ns0:hi> with Food; a Metaphor from the fatting of Cattel with Grass or Hay. The same Wor<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> is used, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 14.20. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 6.42. <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 4.12. These two good Wishes answer the two former great Wants.</ns0:note>, nothwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstand, <ns0:hi>when yet ye are able to relieve them</ns0:hi>; for he speaks to the Rich, or such as were in a capacity of being helpful to others.</ns0:note>: what <ns0:hi>doth it</ns0:hi> profit <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Either what do your good Words, and charitable Wishes profit them, without charitable Deeds? Or, what do they profit your selves? or both may be included: As your fair Speeches convey no real Good to them, so they bring in no Reward to you from God.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 Even so faith <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">That which they boasted of, and called Faith.</ns0:note>, if it hath not works, is dead <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Void of that Life, in which the very Essence of Faith consists, and which always discovers it self in Vital actings, and good Fruits, where it is not hindred by some forceable Impediment; in Allusion to a Corps, which plainly appears to have no vital Principle in it, all vital Operations being ceased. It resem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bles a Man's Body, and is called so, but in reality is not so, but a dead Carkase.</ns0:note>, being <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:hi>by it self.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> alone <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Margin, <ns0:hi>by it self,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> it self, be it what it will, it is but dead; or, as we render it, <ns0:hi>being alone,</ns0:hi> i. e. not in conjunction with Works, which always it should be.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 Yea, a man <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Any true Believer.</ns0:note> may say <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">To any such boasting Hypocrite.</ns0:note>, Thou hast faith <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Thou pretendest to have Faith, or admit thou hast Faith; and an Historical Faith he might have, as <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 19.</ns0:note>, and I have works <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">I do not boast of my Faith, or to say nothing of my Faith, yet Works I do profess to have.</ns0:note>: shew me thy faith <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                     <ns0:hi>Some Copies re<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>d,</ns0:hi> by thy works.</ns0:note> with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />out thy works <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">There be two Readings of these Words, but in both the sense agrees with the rest of the Apostles Discourse. If we take the marginal Reading, shew me thy Faith <ns0:hi>by</ns0:hi> thy Works, the sense is, Evidence the Faith thou pretendest to, by thy Works, as the Fruits of it; let thy Actions vouch for thy Profession. But if we take the Reading in the Text, <ns0:hi>without</ns0:hi> thy Works, it is a kind of Iro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nical Expression, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> make it appear by convincing Argu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments, that thou hast true Faith, when yet thou wantest Works, the only Argument of the Truth of it; understand here, <ns0:hi>but this thou canst not.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, and I will shew thee my faith by my works <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">I will easily prove my Faith to be true and genuine, by those good Works it brings forth in me. Demonstrate the Cause to me without the Effect, if thou canst; but I will easily demonstrate the Cause by the Effect, and prove the Root of Faith to be in me, by my bringing forth that Fruit which is proper to it. It cannot hence be inferred, that wherever such Works are, as Men count, and call good, there must needs be Faith: The Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle's meaning only is, That wherever true Faith is, there good Works will certainly be.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 Thou believest that there is one God <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Thou givest thy Assent to this Truth, that there is one God. This may likewise imply other Articles of the Creed, to which the like Assent may be given.</ns0:note>, thou dost well <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Either this kind of Faith hath its goodness, tho it be not saving, or ironically <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> a great matter thou dost, when thou goest almost as high as the Devils.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mark 1.24.</ns0:note> The devils also believe <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Yield the like Assent to the same Truth.</ns0:note>, and tremble <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The word signifies extreme Fear and Horror, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> such as the thoughts of their Judge strikes into them. This shews the Faith the Apostle speaks of in this place, not to be the Faith of God's Elect, which begets in Believers an holy Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fidence in God, and frees them from slavish Fears; whereas the Faith here spoken of, if it have any Effect upon Men, it is <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ut to fill them with Horror.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 But wilt thou know <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Either this Question is in order to reaching, as <ns0:hi>Iob.</ns0:hi> 13.12. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 13.3. and then the sense is, <ns0:hi>If thou hast a mind to know, I shall instruct thee</ns0:hi>: Or, it is a teaching by way of Que<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stion, as more emphatical, and pressing; and then it is, as if he had said, <ns0:hi>know, O vain Man.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, O vain man <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">An Allusion to an empty Vessel, which founds more than one that is full. The carnal Professor to whom he speaks, is vain, because empty of true Faith, and good Works, tho full of noise and boasting. <ns0:hi>Obj.</ns0:hi> Doth not the Apostle sin against Christ's Command, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 5.22? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> 1. He speaks not of any particular Man, but to all in general, of such a sort, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> who boasted of their Faith, and yet did not evidence it by their VVorks. 2. It is not spoken in rash anger, or by way of Contempt, but by way of Correction and just Reproof; see the like spoken by Christ himself, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 23.17, 19. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 24.25. and by <ns0:hi>Paul,</ns0:hi> Gal. 3.1. and 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15.36.</ns0:note>, that faith vvwithout vvorks <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">A defective Speech, <ns0:hi>Faith without Works</ns0:hi>; for that <ns0:hi>Faith which is without Works,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Faith, if it be without Works.</ns0:hi> He doth not say, <ns0:hi>Faith is dead without Works,</ns0:hi> lest it should be thought that VVorks were the cause of the Life of Faith; but <ns0:hi>Faith without Works is dead,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 17, and 26. implying, that VVorks are the Ef<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fects and Signs of the life of Faith.</ns0:note> is dead?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 Was not Abraham our father <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Not only the Father of us, as <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> (for to them he wrote) and according to the Flesh, but as Believers, and according to the Promise; so all Believers are called <ns0:hi>Abra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ham</ns0:hi>'s Children, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 4.11. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 3.7.</ns0:note> justified <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Found, or decla<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />red to be justified, not only before God, but in the Face of the VVorld; and his Faith (by which he had been justi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fied above thirty years before, in the sight of God) now approved as a true, lively, justifying Faith, by this Proof he gave of it, upon God's trying him in the offering up his Son, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 22.9, 12. <ns0:hi>Now I know that thou fearest God,</ns0:hi> &c. <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> did fear God, and believe him before, and was justified before in the sight of God, but by the working of his Faith in so eminent an Act of Obedience, the Sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerity of all his Graces, and so of his Faith, was manifested, and made known, and so his Faith it self justified, as his Per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son was before, and he obtained this ample Testimony from the Mouth of God himself. So that <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi>'s Justification here, was not the Absolution of a Sinner, but the solemn Approbation of a Believer; not a justifying him as ungodly, but commending him for his Godliness. He was by his Works justified as a righteous person, but not made righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous, or constituted in a justified state, by his Works. The Design of the Apostle is not to shew how Sinners are justi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fied in God's Court, but only what kind of Faith it is where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />by they are justified, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> such a one as purifies the Heart, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 15.9. and looks to Christ, not only as made Righteous<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, but Sanctification to them, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.30. and consequent<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly not only rests on him for Justification, but stirs them up to yield Obedience to him.</ns0:note> by works when he had offered <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> in his firm Purpose and Resolution, and was about to do it actually, had not God hindred him. It was no fault in <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> that it was not actually done, and therefore it was counted to him, as if it had been really done, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 22.12. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 11.17.</ns0:note> Isaac his son upon the altar <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">This shews the setled purpose of <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> to sacrifice <ns0:hi>Isaac,</ns0:hi> when he proceeded so far as to bind him, and lay him upon the Altar; for that argues, that he expected, and intended no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing but his Death, which generally was wont to follow in Sacrifices, when once laid upon the Altar.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>than seest.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> Seest thou <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Heb. 11.17.</ns0:note> how faith wrought with his works <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">He doth not say, <ns0:hi>works wrought with his Faith,</ns0:hi> as he should have said, if he had intended their concurrence in Ju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stification; but <ns0:hi>Faith wrought with his Works,</ns0:hi> i. e. his Faith was not idle, but effectual in producing good Works, it be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the Office and Business of Faith to respect Christ for San<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctification, as well as Righteousness, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 26.18.</ns0:note>, and by works was faith made per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fect <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Either, 1. Faith by producing good Works is it self encouraged, heightned, improved; and so not made perfect by any Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />munication of the Perfection of Works to it, but by being stirred up, and exercised as to the internal Strength and Power of it. Or, 2ly. rather, Faith is made perfect by Works declaratively, in as much as Works evidence, and ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifest the Perfection and Strength of Faith. Faith is the Cause, and Works are the Effects, but the Cause is not per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fected by the Effect, only its Perfection is demonstrated by it, as good Fruit doth not make a Tree good, but shew that it is so. See 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12.9.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 And the scripture was fulfilled <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">This illustrious Instance of <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi>'s Obedience did so clearly evidence the Sincerity of his Faith, that it did most plainly appear, that what the Scripture said of him, it spoke most truly, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> that he did indeed believe God, and it was counted to him for Righteousness. Things are said to be fulfilled when they are most clearly manifested. As those words, <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 2.7. <ns0:hi>This day have I begotten thee,</ns0:hi> are said to be fulfilled at Christ's Resurrection, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 13.32, 33 not the he was then first begotten of the Father, but that he was then in a glorious manner declared to be the Son of God by the Resurrection from the dead, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.4. So here <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi>'s of<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fering up his Son being the evident Discovery of his Faith, it did by that appear, that the Scripture-report of him was true, that <ns0:hi>he believed God,</ns0:hi> &c. he did believe before, and his Faith was imputed to him before, but it was never so fully made known, as by this so high an act of Obedience.</ns0:note>, which saith, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 15.6. Rom. 4.3. Gal. 3.6.</ns0:note> Abraham believed God, and it was im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />puted to him for righteousness <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> as apprehending Christ in the Promise, Faith is said to be imputed for Righteousness, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 4.3, 5, 6. as being In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />strument or means of applying Christ's Righteousness, by whichb elsewhere we are said to be justified, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 3.24, 25. and 5.19. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5.21. <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 3.9.</ns0:note>; and he was cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">2 Chro. 20.7. Isa. 41.8.</ns0:note> Friend of God <ns0:note n="p." place="bottom">Either <ns0:hi>he was the Friend of God</ns0:hi>; to be called, sometimes implies as much as to be, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 48.8. or properly he was called, 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 20.7. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 41.8. and that not only on the account of God's fre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quent Appearances to him, conversing with him, revealing Secrets to him, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 18.17, 18. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 15.15. and entring into Covenant with him, but especially his renewing the Cove<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nant with him, upon the sacrificing of his Son, and confirm<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing it by Oath, and thereby, as it were, admitting him into a nearer degree of Friendship, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 22.16. &c.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:575" />24 Ye see then <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">An Inference either from the Instance of <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> or from the whole preceding Discourse.</ns0:note> how that by works <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Works of new Obedience-</ns0:note> a man is justified <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Declared to be righteous, or approved as such, and acquitted from the Guilt of Hypocrisie.</ns0:note>, and not by faith only <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Not by a meer Profession of Faith, or a bare assent to the Truth, with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />out the Fruit of good Works. <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> How doth this general Conclusion follow from the particular Case of <ns0:hi>Abraham? Ans. Abraham</ns0:hi>'s Faith and Justification both before God, and the World, are set forth as the Exemplars of ours, to which the Faith and Justification of all Believers, both <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> and Gentiles, is to be conformed, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 4.11, 12, 23, 24. <ns0:hi>Q.</ns0:hi> Doth not <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> here contradict <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi>'s Doctrine in the matter of Justification, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 4? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> The Contradiction is but seeming, not real, as will appear, if four things be considered: 1. The occasion of these Apostles Writing, and their Scope in it: Having to do with different sorts of Persons, they had like<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wise different Designs. As Christ speaks one way when he dealt with proud <ns0:hi>Pharisees,</ns0:hi> whom he would humble; ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther way, when with humble Hearers whom he would en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />courage: And <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> carried it one way when among weak Brethren, in Condescention to whose Infirmities he circum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cised <ns0:hi>Timothy,</ns0:hi> Acts 16.2, 3. and another, when he was among false Brethren, and Men of Contention, who opposed Chri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stian Liberty, seeking to bring Believers into Bondage, and then would not suffer <ns0:hi>Titus</ns0:hi> to be circumcised, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 2.3, 4, 5 So in the present Affair, <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi>'s Business lay with false Apostles and Judaizing Christians, such as did, in the matter of Ju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stification, either substitute a Self-righteousness instead of God's Grace, or set it up in Conjunction with it; and there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore his Scope is (especially in his Epistles to the <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Galatians</ns0:hi>) to shew the true cause and manner of Justification, and vindicate the freeness of Grace in it, by the Exclusion of Man's Works of what kind soever; to which purpose he propounds the Examples of <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> in their Justification, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 4. Whereas <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> having to do with carnal Professors, and such as abused the Doctrine of Grace, to encourage themselves in Sin, and thought it suffi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cient that they had Faith, (such as it was) tho they did not live like Believers, resting in an empty Profession, with the neglect of Holiness; his Design plainly is to shew the Effects and Fruits of Justification, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> Holiness and good Works; thereby to check the Vanity and Folly of them, who did thus divorce Faith from an holy Life, (which God hath joyned to it) and fansied themselves safe in the Profession of the one, without any respect to, or care of the other, as ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pears in this Chapter, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 14, 17, 26. And because they might bear themselves high in this false Confidence, by the Ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ample of <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> their Father according to the Flesh, and whom <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> had set forth, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 4. as justified by Faith, with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />out the concurrence of Works to his Justification; <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> makes use of the same Example of <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> as one eminent for Holiness, as well as Faith; and who made his Faith fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mous by the highest Act of Obedience that ever a Saint did, to shew, that Faith and Holiness ought not to be separated; <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi>'s Faith being so highly commended, especially as productive of it. To the same purpose he makes use of the Instance of <ns0:hi>Rahab,</ns0:hi> who tho a young Saint, and newly come to the Knowledge of God, yet shewed the truth of her Faith by so considerable an Exercise of her Love and Mercy to God's People, as her receiving the Spies in Peace, was. This therefore helps not a little to reconcile the difference between these two Apostles. <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> deals with those that magnified Works too much, as if they were justified by them, and slighted Faith and Grace; and therefore tho he frequently shews the usefulness of Faith and good Works unto Salva<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, and presseth Men every where to the Practice of them, yet he proves, that they have no Interest in the Justification of a Sinner before God's Tribunal, which he asserts to be wholly and solely of Grace, and by Faith. But <ns0:hi>Iames,</ns0:hi> in dealing with loose Christians, who magnified Faith, and slighted good Works, not only as having no Influence on Justification, but as not necessary at all to Salvation; he takes upon him to maintain good Works, not as necessary to Ju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stification, but as the Effects, Signs, and Evidences of it, and such as without which their Faith was vain, and themselves in an unjustified state. 2ly. <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> take Faith in different senses; <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> speaks of a true, lively Faith, which purifies the Heart, and works by love, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 5, 6. Whereas <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> speaks of a Profession, or Presumption of Faith, bar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ren, and destitute of good Fruits, such a Faith as is dead, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 17. such as the Devils may have, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 19. which is but Historical, and consists only in a Belief of God's Being, not a consent to his Offer, or relying on his Promises. What Contradi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ction then is there here between these two Apostles, if <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> assert Justification to be by Faith, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> a lively, work<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing Faith, and <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> deny it to be by Faith, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> an idle, unactive, barren Faith, and which hath only the Name, but not the Nature of that Grace, and is rather the Image of Faith than Faith it self? 3ly. But because <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> not only denies Ju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stification to the Faith he speaks of, but ascribes it to Works in this Verse; therefore it is to be considered, that Justifica<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion is taken one way by him, and another by <ns0:hi>Paul: Paul</ns0:hi> takes it for the Absolution, and Acceptation of a Sinner at God's Bar, by the Imputation of Christ's Righteousness, which is the primary and proper Notion of Justification. But <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> takes it for the Manifestation and Declaration of that Justification; and the Word is taken in the like sense in other Scriptures, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 7.29. the People <ns0:hi>justified</ns0:hi> God, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> owned and declared his Righteousness by Confession of their Sins, and Submission to <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi>'s Baptism; and <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 35. <ns0:hi>Wisdom is justified,</ns0:hi> i. e. declared to be just and right, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 3.4. <ns0:hi>justified in thy Sayings,</ns0:hi> i. e. acknowledged and declared to be true in thy Word. And what is Christ's being <ns0:hi>justified in the Spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit,</ns0:hi> 1 Tim 3.16. but his being declared to be the Son of God? <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.4. And that <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> takes Justification in this sense, appears, 1. by the History of <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> here mentioned: he was (as hath been said) justified by Faith long before his offering up his Son, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 15. but here is said to be justi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fied, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> declared and proved to be so by this Testimony which he gave to the Truth of his Faith, and consequently to his Justification by it; and the Lord therefore tells him, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 22.12. <ns0:hi>Now I know that thou fearest me,</ns0:hi> &c. <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> by this Obedience thou hast abundantly shewed the Sincerity of thy Graces. 2. Because if <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> doth not here speak of <ns0:hi>Abra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ham</ns0:hi>'s being justified declaratively, how can it be true which he speaks, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 23. that the <ns0:hi>Scripture was fulfilled</ns0:hi> (in his sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />crificing his Son) which saith, <ns0:hi>
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e believed God, and it was imputed to him for Righteousness?</ns0:hi> For if <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> intends Justi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fication in the proper sense, how was <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi>'s being justi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fied by Works, a fulfilling of the Scripture, which asserts him to be justified by Faith? Here therefore again there is no Contradiction between these Apostles. For it is true, that <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> was justified, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> accepted of God, and ab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />solved from Guilt, by Faith only: And it is as true, that he was justified, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> manifested and declared to be a Belie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver, and a justified Person by his Works. 4ly. Lastly, we may distinguish of the Person that is said to be justified, either he is a Sinner, in the state of Nature; or a Believer in a state of Grace; whence ariseth the two-fold Justifica<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion here mentiond. The Justification of a Sinner in the Remission of his Sins through the Imputation of Christ's Righteousness, and acquitting him from the Condemnation of the Law, is the Justification properly so called, and which <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> speaks so much of<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and this is by Faith only. The Justification of a Believer, is his Absolution from Condem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nation by the Gospel, and the charge of Infidelity, or Hy<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pocrisie, and is no other than that declarative Justification <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> speaks of, or an asserting, and clearing up the truth and reality of the former Justification, which is done by good Works, as the Signs and Fruits of the Faith, by which that former is obtained; and this is but improperly called Justification. The former is an Absolution from the general Charge of Sin, this from the special charge of Hypocrisie, or Infidelity: A Sinner's great fear (when first awakened to a sense of his Sin and Misery) is of an holy Law, and a righteous Judge ready to condemn him for the Violation of that Law; and so his first Business is to look to Christ by Faith for Righteousness, and Remission of Sin. But when he is justified by that Righteousness, Men may charge him with Hypocrisie, or Unbelief; and so may the Devil and Conscience too, when Faith is weak, or a Temptation strong; and therefore his next Work is to clear himself of this Im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />putation, and to evidence the truth and reality of his Faith and Justification in God's sight, which must be done by producing his Obedience and good Works, as the Indicati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons of his Faith; and hereby he proves, that he hath in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deed closed with the Promise of the Gospel, and so is clear of the Charge of not believing it, which was false; as well as (by Consequence) is justified from the Charge of Sin a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst the Law, which was true. To conclude, therefore, here is no opposition between <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iames. Paul</ns0:hi> speaks of <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi>'s being justified as a Sinner, and properly, and so by Faith only: <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> speaks of his being justified as a Believer, improperly, and so by Works; by which not his Person was justified, but rather his Faith declared to be justifying; nor he constituted righteous, but approved as righteous. In a Word, what God hath joyned, must not be divided; and what he hath divided, must not be joyned. He hath separated Faith and Works in the Business of Justi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fication, and therefore we must not joyn them in it, as <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> disputes; and he hath joyned them in the Lives of justified Persons, and there we must not separate them, as <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> teaches. <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> assures us they have not a <ns0:hi>co-efficiency</ns0:hi> in Justification it self; and <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> assures us they may, and ought to have a <ns0:hi>co-existence</ns0:hi> in them that are justified. If the Reader desire further Satisfaction yet, let him consult <ns0:hi>Turre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tine de Concordia Pauli & Iacobi,</ns0:hi> where he may find much more to the same purpose, as hath been here said.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:576" />25 Likewise also was not Rahab <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">This Instance of <ns0:hi>Rahab</ns0:hi> is joyned to that of <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> either to shew, that none of any Condition, Degree, or Na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, was ever numbred among true Believers; without good Works, or else to prove, that Faith, wherever it is sincere and genuine, is likewise operative, and fruitful, not only in older Disciples and stronger, such as <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> was, but even proportionably in those that are weaker, and but newly converted to the Faith, which was <ns0:hi>Rahab</ns0:hi>'s case.</ns0:note> the har<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lot <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Really and properly so, <ns0:hi>Iosh.</ns0:hi> 2.1. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 11.31. tho possibly she might keep an Inn, and that might occasion the Spies go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to her House, not knowing her to be one of so scan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dalous a Life; which yet the Holy Ghost takes special notice of, that by the Infamousness of her former Conversation, the Grace of God in her Conversion might be more conspicu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous.</ns0:note> justified by works <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">In the same sense as <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> was, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> declared to be righteous, and her Sincerity approved in the Face of the Congregation of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> when, upon her hiding the Spies, God gave a Commandment to save her alive, though the rest of her People were to be destroyed.</ns0:note>, when she had recei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved the messengers, and had sent them out ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther way?<ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Her recei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving them implies likewise her hiding them; both which, together with her sending them forth another way, were Acts of Love to the People of God, of Mercy to the Spies, and of great Self-denial in respect of her own Safety, which the hazarded by thus exposing her self to the Fury of the King of <ns0:hi>Iericho,</ns0:hi> and her Countrymen; but all proceed<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed from her Faith in the God of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> of whose great Works she had heard, and whom she had now taken to be her God, and under whose Wings she was now come to trust.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 For as the body without the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>breath.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> spirit <ns0:note n="*" place="bottom">This may be understood either according to the mar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ginal reading, of the <ns0:hi>Breath,</ns0:hi> and then the sense is, that Life and Breath being inseparable Companions, as the want of Breath argues want of Life in the Body; so lively Faith and Works being as infeparable, want of Works argues want of Lite in Faith: Or, according to the reading in the Text, <ns0:hi>Spirit,</ns0:hi> taking it for that Substance which animates the Body, and is the cause of vital Functions in it, which is sometimes called Spirit, <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 31.5. <ns0:hi>Eccl.</ns0:hi> 12.7. and 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 2.11. and then the sense is, that as a Body is without a Soul, so Faith is without Works, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> both are dead. As a Body with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />out the Soul hath the Shape and Lineaments of a Man, but nothing that may discover Life in it, so Faith without Works may be like true Faith, have some resemblance of it, but hath nothing to discover the Truth and Life of it.</ns0:note> is dead, so faith without works is dead also.<ns0:note n="†" place="bottom">Not true Faith, for that cannot be dead, but an empty Profession of Faith, which is rather called Faith, by way of Conces<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion, or because of some likeness it hath to it, than really is so; as a dead Body, tho called a Body, is really but a Car<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />kase.</ns0:note>
